title: Valence number
competency: Define valence as the combining power of an atom.

keywords.def: The combining power of an element. Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3.
An atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge.

en.text: The combining power of an element is its valence. Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3. Iron, copper, lead and tin have more than one valence. The charge on an ion equals its valence: Cl⁻ has 1, O²⁻ has 2, Al³⁺ has 3.

screens.title: Joining power
screens.ask: Hydrogen joins one other atom. Oxygen can join two hydrogens in H₂O. Which has more "joining power"?
screens.after: Oxygen holds two hydrogens, so it has more combining power. This power is called valence.

screens.title: 3.2.3 Valence number
paras: Each element in a compound has a combining power.
The combining power of an element is called valence.
If we know the valences, it is easy to write a formula.
Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3.

screens.title: More than one valence
paras: Some elements have more than one valence.
Iron, copper, lead and tin are common examples.
Ions are atoms with a positive or negative charge.
The charge an ion carries equals its valence. Cl⁻, O²⁻ and Al³⁺ have valences 1, 2 and 3.

screens.title: Charge and valence
screens.ask: Tap each ion: the number of charges is its valence.

defs: The combining power of an element. Most common elements have valence 1, 2 or 3.

screens.text: Use Table 3.4: what is the valence of oxygen?
screens.why:
Find oxygen (O) in the non-metal row of Table 3.4.
It is in the valence 2 column, with sulfur.
Its ion O²⁻ also has 2 charges.
Answer: 2.
screens.clue: Look at the non-metal row of Table 3.4.

screens.title: Sort by valence
screens.why:
Valence 1: Na (metal) and Cl (non-metal).
Valence 2: Mg (metal) and O (non-metal).
Valence 3: Al (metal) and N (non-metal).
Each goes by its column in Table 3.4.
screens.text: Sort each element by its valence (Table 3.4).
What is the valence of aluminium?
screens.why:
Find Al in Table 3.4: it is in the valence 3 column.
Its ion is Al³⁺, with 3 charges.
The number of charges equals the valence.
Answer: 3.
screens.clue: Look at the charge on Al³⁺.

screens.text: True or false: iron has only one valence number.
screens.why:
Table 3.4 lists iron twice.
Fe(II) has valence 2. Fe(III) has valence 3.
So iron has two valence numbers.
The statement is false.

screens.text: An ion has the charge 2−. What is its valence?
screens.why:
The valence equals the number of charges.
The sign (+ or −) is not part of the valence.
2− has two charges, so the valence is 2.
Example: O²⁻ has valence 2.
−2 is wrong: a valence is a plain number.

test.text: What is the combining power of an element called?
test.why:
Each element in a compound has a combining power.
This power is called valence.
A symbol is a short name; a formula shows a whole substance.
Answer: valence.

test.text: Use Table 3.4: what is the valence of sodium (Na)?
test.why:
Find Na in the metal row of Table 3.4.
It is in the valence 1 column, with Li and K.
Answer: 1.

test.text: Which element has more than one valence?
test.why:
Sodium has valence 1 only. Oxygen has valence 2 only.
Iron appears as Fe(II) and Fe(III).
So iron has valence 2 and valence 3.
Answer: iron.

test.text: Use Table 3.4: what is the valence of nitrogen?
test.why:
Find N in the non-metal row of Table 3.4.
It is in the valence 3 column.
Answer: 3.

Valence 2 metals: Mg, Ca, Fe(II), Zn, Pb(II).
Valence 2 non-metals: O, S.
So Ca, Zn and S have valence 2.
K and Br have valence 1. Al has valence 3.

notes.text: Exercise 3.3 Q4 asks "How many valence numbers does Aluminium have?"; the intended question is "what is its valence" (answer 3). Used that way.
